deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the previous page): y(x) is an n-valued algebraic function, F(x,y)=0, with branches y_1(x),...,y_n(x). In the complex x-plane (x = u + i v) Hilbert considers the locus C = { x : |y_i(x)| = |y_j(x)| for some i ≠ j }. He asserts that C is an algebraic curve, real-algebraic in (u,v). He also asserts that the branch points of y lie at double points of C.

This page:
(1) The converse fails: not every double point of C is a branch point. For example, an arc where |y_1|=|y_2| can cross an arc where |y_3|=|y_4|, or two arcs belonging to the same pair can cross at an ordinary (non-branch) point.
(2) The double points cut C into arcs ('Stücke').
(3) Labelling. At each x off C, order the roots by modulus: |y_(1)(x)| ≥ |y_(2)(x)| ≥ ... ≥ |y_(n)(x)|. Hilbert says 'der Grösse nach'; the direction of the ordering is immaterial. On an arc of C where the i-th and (i+1)-th roots, in this ordering, have equal modulus, write the integer i on the arc. Only adjacent indices can coincide in modulus on an arc of C, which is why one integer per arc suffices.
(4) The resulting labelled planar picture (the 'Schema') determines the Riemann surface completely. The sketch shows closed and open arcs labelled 1, 5, 2, 4, 3, i. In modern terms [my gloss]: off C the sheets are canonically numbered by modulus rank, so the complement of C gives n single-valued sheets. Crossing an arc labelled i exchanges sheet labels i and i+1, i.e. it acts as the transposition (i i+1). Monodromy around any loop is therefore the product of the transpositions met when crossing C. Branch points are where these labels fail to be globally consistent, and from this one recovers the classical cut/branching data ('Schema der Riemannschen Fläche'). He cites Runge and Fritz Cohn for comparison.
(5) New note. The 'possibility' of Euclidean geometry, i.e. the consistency of its axioms, is easy to show analytically, by representing every point by (as the next page says) 4 homogeneous coordinates. Since non-Euclidean geometry can be modelled analytically in the same way (Cayley–Klein projective metrics), its consistency follows too. The next page adds the wish to imitate this proof purely geometrically.
errors: The claim from the previous page that branch points lie at double points of C is not correct in general. At a simple branch point a, write y_{i,j} = f(t) ± g(t)·sqrt(t) with t = x−a and f(a) ≠ 0. Then |y_i|^2 − |y_j|^2 = 4·Re(conj(f)·g·sqrt(t)) + O(|t|^{3/2}). Its zero set near a is a single half-ray ending at a, so a is an endpoint of an arc of C, not a crossing. Example: y^2 − 2y = x gives y = 1 ± sqrt(1+x). Here |y_1| = |y_2| exactly on x ∈ (−∞, −1], a ray ending at the branch point −1. The statement is only defensible if one passes to the Zariski closure. There the complementary ray (where y_i·conj(y_j) is real) is added, and the closure carries a doubled line through a: the generated real polynomial vanishes to second order there. So 'Doppelpunkt' would need that reinterpretation.

The assertion (previous page) that C is an algebraic curve is imprecise. The function prod_{i<j}(|y_i|^2 − |y_j|^2)^2 is not invariant under the separate permutations of the y_i and of their conjugates, so it is not obviously a polynomial in u, v. A real polynomial is obtained from a product such as prod (y_i·conj(y_k) − y_j·conj(y_l)) over index quadruples. Its zero set contains C together with extra components, so C is a semi-algebraic subset of a real algebraic curve.
Degenerate cases are ignored. If f ≡ 0 for some pair (e.g. y^2 = x), then |y_1| = |y_2| everywhere and the scheme breaks down.

The claim that the labelled scheme 'vollständig ersetzt' the Riemann surface is stated without proof. It is plausible via the transposition-monodromy interpretation, but the reader is referred to Runge and Cohn.

results.what: Encoding the Riemann surface of an algebraic function by the planar locus |y_i(x)| = |y_{i+1}(x)|, with roots ordered by modulus and arcs labelled by the index i. Crossing an arc labelled i swaps sheets i and i+1.
results.modern_name: A combinatorial (cut-system / monodromy) description of a branched covering by adjacent transpositions, with sheets ordered by root modulus. It is related to modulus-ordering ideas in amoebas and Graeffe/Newton-polygon methods, and to algorithmic monodromy computation.
results.usually_credited_to: Unsure. Comparable ideas appear in Runge's work and possibly in Fritz Cohn's, as Hilbert himself notes; classical cut systems go back to Riemann, Neumann, Clebsch–Gordan, Lüroth and Hurwitz.

results.what: Consistency of the axioms of Euclidean (and hence non-Euclidean) geometry via an analytic coordinate model with homogeneous coordinates.
results.modern_name: Relative consistency proof via an analytic (arithmetical) model; Cayley–Klein models for non-Euclidean geometry.
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert, Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), building on Beltrami (1868), Klein (1871) and Cayley (1859).

deep.surprise_reason: The geometry note is the well-known germ of Hilbert's consistency program, which appears in the Grundlagen. The Riemann-surface idea, ordering sheets by root modulus and encoding the surface by labelled curves |y_i| = |y_{i+1}|, is a pleasant unpublished research idea. However, Hilbert attributes related work to Runge and Cohn, and it contains an inaccuracy about branch points being double points. It is notable mainly as a sketch, not a major unrecognized result.

checkable.asserts: Equals 4*a. So for y = 1 ± s with s = sqrt(1+x), |y_1| = |y_2| iff Re(s) = 0, i.e. iff 1+x ≤ 0: a ray ending at the branch point x = −1, not a double point.
The roots are 1 - sqrt(x+1) and 1 + sqrt(x+1), so the example used above is correct.

checkable.sympy: f,g,s=symbols('f g s'); fb,gb,sb=symbols('fb gb sb'); expand((f+g*s)*(fb+gb*sb)-(f-g*s)*(fb-gb*sb))
checkable.asserts: Equals 2*(fb*g*s + f*gb*sb) = 4*Re(conj(f)*g*s), with conjugates written as fb, gb, sb. This is the local form of |y_i|^2 − |y_j|^2 near a branch point.

checkable.sympy: f,g,s=symbols('f g s'); fb,gb,sb=symbols('fb gb sb'); expand((f+g*s)*(fb-gb*sb)-(f-g*s)*(fb+gb*sb))
checkable.asserts: Equals 2*(fb*g*s - f*gb*sb) = 4*I*Im(conj(f)*g*s), whose zero set is the complementary ray added in the Zariski closure.
